CHAPTER 3.3 · LEARNING AREA 3

CHAPTER 3.3 · LEARNING AREA 3 · MARCH · APRIL

Area and the house of quadrilaterals

How big is a slanting flower bed, a triangular sail or a plot of land with a crooked boundary? You learn the trick for working out almost any area: cut up, move, fill in, until you get a rectangle. After that you sort all quadrilaterals into a house in which every floor can do more than the one below.

10 LESSONS3 UNITS2 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • calculate the perimeter and area of a parallelogram and a triangle
  • derive and apply the formulas for the trapezium and the kite
  • cut up or fill in composite figures
  • sort triangles and quadrilaterals by their properties: the house of quadrilaterals

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Parallelogram and triangle

If you cut a triangle off the parallelogram at right angles and put it on the other side, you get a rectangle. It is as long as the base $g$ and as high as the height $h$ of the parallelogram. The area has not changed.

Important: the height is always perpendicular to the base. The slanting side is not the height.

A triangle is exactly half a parallelogram: if you rotate a copy about the midpoint of one side, the two together make a parallelogram. Any side can be the base, and it then has its own height.

The perimeter is the length of the boundary, that is the sum of all the sides.

KEY POINT · PARALLELOGRAM AND TRIANGLE

Parallelogram: $A = g \cdot h$

Triangle: $A = \tfrac12 \cdot g \cdot h$

Perimeter: the sum of all side lengths. For the parallelogram $u = 2a + 2b$.

The height $h$ is perpendicular to the base $g$ (or to its extension).

Obtuse triangle: the height can lie outside. Then you extend the base and drop the perpendicular onto it.

Units: cm times cm gives cm². Both lengths must have the same unit.

INTERACTIVE · CUT AND MOVE

Push “Cut and move” to 100%. Then switch to the triangle: the copy rotates about the midpoint of a side.

EXAMPLE 1 · A FLOWER BED

A flower bed has the shape of a parallelogram with $g = 6$ m and $h = 3.5$ m. The slanting sides are 4 m long. Calculate the area and the perimeter.

$A = 6 \cdot 3.5 = 21$ m². $u = 2 \cdot 6 + 2 \cdot 4 = 20$ m.

21 m² area, 20 m perimeter. You only need the 4 m for the perimeter.

EXAMPLE 2 · A SAIL

A triangular sail has a bottom edge of $2.4$ m, the mast is $5$ m high and stands perpendicular to it. How big is the sail?

The mast is the height to the bottom edge: $A = \tfrac12 \cdot 2.4 \cdot 5$.

$A = 6$ m²

EXERCISES

Calculate the area: a) parallelogram $g = 8$ cm, $h = 5$ cm   b) triangle $g = 7$ cm, $h = 4$ cm   c) triangle $g = 3.5$ m, $h = 2$ m   d) parallelogram $g = 12$ mm, $h = 2.5$ cm

In d) first convert to the same unit.

a) 40 cm²   b) 14 cm²   c) $3.5$ m²   d) $1.2 \cdot 2.5 = 3$ cm²

A triangle has an area of 24 cm² and a base of 8 cm. How high is it? How high would a parallelogram with the same area and base be?

Triangle: $24 = \tfrac12 \cdot 8 \cdot h$, so $h = 6$ cm. Parallelogram: $24 = 8 \cdot h$, so $h = 3$ cm.

Draw different triangles with $g = 6$ cm and $h = 4$ cm. What do you notice about the areas? Which has the smallest perimeter?

All have 12 cm², wherever the apex lies on the parallel. The isosceles triangle, with the apex exactly above the midpoint, has the smallest perimeter.

In a triangle $c = 10$ cm with $h_c = 6$ cm, and $a = 8$ cm. How long is the height $h_a$?

The area is the same whichever side you take as the base.

$A = \tfrac12 \cdot 10 \cdot 6 = 30$ cm². $30 = \tfrac12 \cdot 8 \cdot h_a$, so $h_a = 7.5$ cm.

A parallelogram has the sides 6 cm and 4 cm. At most how big can its area be? How small can it get?

Largest when it is a rectangle: 24 cm². If you tilt it flatter and flatter, the height gets smaller and smaller: the area can become as small as you like, but never quite 0.

Parallelogram with $g = 6$ m and $h = 3.5$ m. Area?

$6 \cdot 3.5 = 21$

Sail with edge $2.4$ m and height 5 m. Area?

$\tfrac12 \cdot 2.4 \cdot 5 = 6$

Triangle with 30 cm² and $a = 8$ cm. How long is $h_a$?

$60 : 8 = 7.5$

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Trapezium, kite and composite figures

Two identical trapeziums, one of them turned round, fit together into a parallelogram. Its base is $a + c$, its height $h$. So a trapezium is half of it. For the kite a rectangle made from the two diagonals helps: the kite fills exactly half of it.

This is the principle of reduction: a new figure is traced back to a known one. That is also how you calculate composite figures: you cut them into rectangles, triangles and trapeziums, or you fill them in to make a large figure and subtract what is too much.

KEY POINT · TRAPEZIUM AND KITE

Trapezium with the parallel sides $a$ and $c$ and the height $h$: $A = \tfrac12 \cdot (a + c) \cdot h$

Kite and rhombus with the diagonals $e$ and $f$: $A = \tfrac12 \cdot e \cdot f$

Composite: cut up and add, or fill in and subtract.

Memory aid for the trapezium: $\tfrac12 (a + c)$ is the mean width. Mean width times height, as for the rectangle.

Square as a rhombus: $A = \tfrac12 \cdot e \cdot f$ also holds for the square. With the diagonal 4 cm: $\tfrac12 \cdot 4 \cdot 4 = 8$ cm².

INTERACTIVE · TRAPEZIUM AND KITE

For the trapezium a copy rotates to make a parallelogram. Then choose “Kite”: the four triangles fold outwards.

EXAMPLE 3 · A DYKE

The cross-section of a dyke is a trapezium: 8 m wide at the bottom, 4 m wide at the top, 3 m high. What is the area of the cross-section?

$A = \tfrac12 \cdot (8 + 4) \cdot 3 = 6 \cdot 3$.

18 m²

EXAMPLE 4 · FILLING IN

An L-shaped terrace: 7 m by 5 m on the outside, a rectangle of 3 m by 2 m is missing from one corner. How big is it?

Fill in to make the large rectangle and subtract the missing piece: $7 \cdot 5 - 3 \cdot 2 = 35 - 6$.

29 m²

EXERCISES

a) trapezium: $a = 9$ cm, $c = 5$ cm, $h = 4$ cm   b) kite: $e = 6$ cm, $f = 10$ cm   c) rhombus: $e = 5$ cm, $f = 5$ cm

a) $\tfrac12 \cdot 14 \cdot 4 = 28$ cm²   b) $30$ cm²   c) $12.5$ cm² (that is a square)

The kite from the exploration has sticks of 60 cm and 80 cm. What is the least amount of fabric you need?

$\tfrac12 \cdot 60 \cdot 80 = 2400$ cm² $= 0.24$ m².

A plot of land has the shape of a trapezium. The parallel sides are 40 m and 25 m long, their distance apart is 30 m. 1 m² costs €120. What does the plot cost?

$A = \tfrac12 \cdot 65 \cdot 30 = 975$ m². Price: $975 \cdot 120 = 117{,}000$, so €117,000.

The gable end of a house consists of a rectangle (8 m wide, 5 m high) with a triangle on top (8 m wide, 3 m high). It has a window of $1.5$ m by $1.2$ m. What area has to be painted?

$8 \cdot 5 + \tfrac12 \cdot 8 \cdot 3 - 1.5 \cdot 1.2 = 40 + 12 - 1.8 = 50.2$ m².

Show: the trapezium formula also works for the parallelogram ($c = a$) and for the triangle ($c = 0$).

$c = a$: $\tfrac12 \cdot (a + a) \cdot h = a \cdot h$, the formula for the parallelogram. $c = 0$: $\tfrac12 \cdot a \cdot h$, the formula for the triangle.

$6 \cdot 3 = 18$

Kite with $e = 6$ cm, $f = 10$ cm. Area?

$\tfrac12 \cdot 60$

Rectangle 7 m by 5 m, without a corner of 3 m by 2 m. Area?

$35 - 6$

UNIT 32 LESSONS

3The house of quadrilaterals

A rectangle is a quadrilateral with four right angles. The square has four right angles, so every square is a rectangle. It even has more: four sides of equal length. The other way round, not every rectangle is a square.

Mathematicians sort figures by their properties. This is called classifying. For the quadrilaterals you get a picture like a house: at the very bottom the general quadrilateral, at the very top the square. Every quadrilateral inherits all the properties of the quadrilaterals below it.

Triangles can be sorted too: by their sides (scalene, isosceles, equilateral) or by their angles (acute, right-angled, obtuse). Every equilateral triangle is also isosceles.

KEY POINT · SORTING QUADRILATERALS

Trapezium: at least one pair of parallel sides.   Parallelogram: two pairs of parallel sides.

Rectangle: parallelogram with four right angles.   Rhombus: parallelogram with four sides of equal length.

Square: rectangle and rhombus at the same time.   Kite: two pairs of equal adjacent sides.

Proving a property: in a parallelogram a diagonal divides it into two congruent triangles (ASA with alternate angles). That is why opposite sides are equal in length.

Language: “Every square is a rectangle” is true. “Every rectangle is a square” is false.

INTERACTIVE · THE HOUSE OF QUADRILATERALS

Tap a quadrilateral. Everything else it also is lights up orange. Its properties are on the right.

EXAMPLE 5 · TRUE OR FALSE?

“Every rhombus is a kite.”

A rhombus has four sides of equal length. Then each pair of adjacent sides is of equal length.

true. The other way round, not every kite is a rhombus.

EXAMPLE 6 · SORTING TRIANGLES

Can a triangle be isosceles and right-angled? Equilateral and right-angled?

Isosceles and right-angled: yes, with the angles $90^\circ$, $45^\circ$, $45^\circ$. Equilateral has three $60^\circ$ angles, so never a right angle.

yes · no

EXERCISES

True or false? a) Every rectangle is a parallelogram. b) Every trapezium is a parallelogram. c) Every square is a rhombus. d) Every parallelogram is a trapezium.

a) true   b) false   c) true   d) true

Which quadrilateral is meant? a) The diagonals are equal in length and bisect each other, but are not perpendicular. b) The diagonals are perpendicular and bisect each other, but are of different lengths.

a) rectangle (not a square)   b) rhombus (not a square)

Justify with a congruence theorem: in a parallelogram $ABCD$ the opposite sides are equal in length.

Draw the diagonal $\overline{AC}$ and look for alternate angles.

The diagonal $\overline{AC}$ belongs to both triangles $ABC$ and $CDA$. Because $AB \parallel CD$, $\angle BAC$ and $\angle DCA$ are alternate angles, so they are equal. Because $BC \parallel AD$, $\angle BCA$ and $\angle DAC$ are equal. By ASA the triangles are congruent, so $\overline{AB} = \overline{CD}$ and $\overline{BC} = \overline{DA}$.

TEST YOURSELF!

How many lines of symmetry does a square have?

Four: two diagonals and two midlines.

How many pairs of parallel sides does a rhombus have?

Two, it is a parallelogram.

A triangle is isosceles and right-angled. How big is a base angle?

$90^\circ : 2 = 45^\circ$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Convert: a) $3.5$ m² to dm²   b) 450 cm² to dm²   c) $0.2$ ha to m² (1 ha = 10,000 m²)

a) 350 dm²   b) $4.5$ dm²   c) 2000 m²

Connecting with chapter 2.2: a parallelogram is to have an area of 36 cm². Make a table for the base and the height. What kind of assignment is this?

For example 3 → 12, 4 → 9, 6 → 6, 9 → 4, 12 → 3. $g \cdot h = 36$ is always the same: inversely proportional.

Connecting with chapter 1.2: a trapezium has $a = 4\tfrac12$ cm, $c = 2\tfrac14$ cm and $h = 2$ cm. Calculate the area with fractions.

$\tfrac12 \cdot \left(\tfrac92 + \tfrac94\right) \cdot 2 = \tfrac{27}{4} = 6\tfrac34$ cm²

If you halve the base of a triangle and double its height, what happens to the area? And if you double both?

Half the base and double the height: the same area. Both doubled: four times the area.

EXCURSIONA BEAUTIFUL THEOREM

Areas by counting

On squared paper draw a polygon whose corners all lie on grid points. Then you can find its area without any formula, just by counting:

Count the grid points inside ($I$) and the grid points on the boundary ($R$). Then: $A = I + \tfrac{R}{2} - 1$ (in squares).

The Austrian mathematician Georg Pick found this theorem in Prague in 1899. For almost seventy years hardly anyone knew it. Only when the Polish mathematician Hugo Steinhaus included it in his famous book “Mathematical Snapshots” in 1969 did it become well known.

Check it: a rectangle of 3 by 2 squares has 2 grid points inside and 10 on the boundary. Does the formula work?

$A = 2 + \tfrac{10}{2} - 1 = 6$ squares. And $3 \cdot 2 = 6$ ✓

Source: Georg Pick, “Geometrisches zur Zahlenlehre”, Sitzungsberichte des Vereins Lotos, Prague, volume 47 (new series 19), 1899, pp. 311–319.

HOUSE OF QUADRILATERALS
